video_title: The Psychology of Losing: Why Winners Add & Losers Hope · Tom Hougaard & David Capablanca
gist: Recorded at a live Chat with Traders event in LA. Tom Hougaard argues that most of his money comes from adding to winners on trend days, rejects fixed targets, and calls prop firms a fee business with a 98-99% failure rate. Small-cap short seller David Capablanca explains how he survives by excluding whole categories (nano floats, Chinese stocks), describes halt and trade-bust tail risks, and lays out graded, seasonal position sizing. Much of the talk is motivational and biographical.

themes.theme: Prop firm economics and failure rates

insights.claim: Tom Hougaard estimates general trading failure rates at 70-80%, but says failure in the prop-account arena runs 98-99%, because prop firms' real business model is collecting monthly evaluation fees.
insights.speaker: Tom Hougaard
insights.so_what: Prop-firm revenue depends on trader failure; treat funded-account offers as a fee business, not a capital partnership.
insights.quote: it's no secret that trading is tough and there's a failure rate of 70 to 80 %, but in the prop arena that failure rate is up at 98 to 99 %

insights.claim: Tom Hougaard argues that many trading podcasters act as customer-acquisition funnels for prop brokers, and he refuses to appear on shows tied to that agenda.
insights.speaker: Tom Hougaard
insights.so_what: Discount trading-media content that monetizes through prop-firm referrals; sponsor incentives shape the narrative that trading is easy.
insights.quote: many of these podcasters, they're simply just funnels for prop brokers

insights.claim: Tom Hougaard believes a young trader is better off building their own capital and learning with it than using prop accounts, which he says bleed traders dry under unfair trading conditions, even in the more regulated US setting.
insights.speaker: Tom Hougaard
insights.so_what: Building your own capital avoids fee drag and conditions stacked against you; this reframes the 'capital is the constraint' pitch.

themes.theme: Small-cap shorting: cut out whole categories

insights.claim: David Capablanca removed entire categories of small caps from his universe (nano-float stocks and Chinese-domiciled stocks) after finding they are the common denominator of the outlier squeezes that end short sellers' careers.
insights.speaker: David Capablanca
insights.so_what: Excluding a whole category cuts off the tail risk of a career-ending squeeze at the cost of a few trades, which is a better trade-off than sizing those names smaller.

insights.claim: David Capablanca says the recent small-cap outlier squeezes cluster in nano-float names, citing floats around 1.6 million shares over the past couple of years.
insights.speaker: David Capablanca
insights.so_what: Screen float size before shorting: sub-~2M floats carry outsized squeeze risk.
insights.quote: Oh, it's the nano floats. Oh, it's actually 1.6 million float uh recently past couple years.

insights.claim: David Capablanca says Chinese small caps ended many trading careers from 2023 to 2026, and he now blocks them out entirely, neither shorting nor going long, because the risk/reward is structurally bad.
insights.speaker: David Capablanca
insights.so_what: Tools that flag where a stock is domiciled (he mentions AI and short-finder tools) let traders filter these names out automatically.
insights.quote: So I don't even look at the Chinese anymore. I block them out. I can't even I can't even see them. It's like they don't exist.

insights.claim: David Capablanca avoids even going long Chinese small caps because of indefinite T12 trading halts: he once had $50,000 locked in a short on a halted Chinese stock for 10 months.
insights.speaker: David Capablanca
insights.so_what: Halt risk traps capital and keeps borrow fees running; liquidity risk applies to longs as well as shorts.
insights.quote: I shorted one Chinese stock 2022. It was [snorts] it was T 12 halted for 10 months. I had I had $50,000 locked up for 10 months

insights.claim: A hedge fund stuck short INHD during a halt or lawsuit told David Capablanca it faced about $1 million in borrow fees in a single month.
insights.speaker: David Capablanca
insights.so_what: Borrow costs during a halt can compound into losses large enough to sink a fund, so model halt duration times borrow rate before shorting illiquid names.
insights.quote: he said I'm going to owe a million dollars in borrow fees this month

insights.claim: Chinese small caps keep producing extreme moves, such as one squeezing from $1 to $37 in the pre-market and WFF going from $1 to $50 in a day, and David Capablanca treats each of these as a reason to stay away, not an opportunity.
insights.speaker: David Capablanca
insights.so_what: Extreme pre-market squeezes in foreign-domiciled micro caps are a hazard to shorts; avoid the setup no matter how stretched it looks.

insights.claim: David Capablanca argues that trading dangerous squeeze-prone names carries an opportunity cost, because it pulls attention away from easier, criteria-fitting shorts such as NCPL, which he shorted from his phone during the conference.
insights.speaker: David Capablanca
insights.so_what: Narrowing the universe improves capital and attention allocation toward high-quality setups.
insights.quote: you're missing opportunities, opportunity costs of the easy stock

themes.theme: Trade busts and exchange tail risk

insights.claim: Exchange trade busts can retroactively wipe out gains: on BYA, trades in roughly the $3.05-and-up range over 4-5 minutes were cancelled, and one trader who kept trading on those phantom profits ended the day deeply down.
insights.speaker: host (Kevin) / David Capablanca
insights.so_what: Don't treat unsettled windfall profits in halted or erratic names as real capital until clearly erroneous trade reviews are resolved.

insights.claim: David Capablanca once lost $25,000 shorting a stock after an erroneous exchange reverse split, and only got the money back when the trade was busted.
insights.speaker: David Capablanca
insights.so_what: Corporate-action errors around reverse splits are a real operational risk for pre-market shorts.

insights.claim: The host cites a small-cap trader with a $30,000 account who ended up owing his broker millions of dollars, an example of the unlimited-loss tail in small-cap shorting.
insights.speaker: host (Kevin)
insights.so_what: On short positions in squeeze-prone names, account size does not cap the loss, so hard exclusion rules matter more than stop placement.

themes.theme: Adding to winners and trend days

insights.claim: Tom Hougaard says most of his money has been made when the market trends and he adds to winning positions, a practice he learned from mentor David Paul.
insights.speaker: Tom Hougaard
insights.so_what: Expectancy comes from pyramiding into trends, not from a high hit rate.
insights.quote: the vast majority of my money has been made on A, the market trending, and B, me adding adding to my positions in a trending market

insights.claim: Tom Hougaard frames the core asymmetry this way: losers add to their losing trades and winners add to their winning trades.
insights.speaker: Tom Hougaard
insights.so_what: Audit your own adds: averaging down is a warning sign, scaling into profit is the edge.
insights.quote: Losers add to their losing trades and winners add to their winning trades.

insights.claim: From almost 10 years watching others on a trading floor, Tom Hougaard concluded that many traders are right 60-70% of the time but blow up on one or two trades because they cannot take a loss.
insights.speaker: Tom Hougaard
insights.so_what: A high win rate means little without loss control, so judge traders and strategies by their worst losses.

insights.claim: Tom Hougaard describes trend days, when the open is the high and the close is the low or the reverse, as the source of outsized returns; during the COVID crash he shorted all day and kept adding on such days.
insights.speaker: Tom Hougaard
insights.so_what: Recognizing a trend day early and pyramiding into it can produce a year's P&L in a session.

insights.claim: Tom Hougaard says that after making more on one trend day than in the previous two years combined, a trader is 'forever damaged' and can't go back to fixed one-to-one targets.
insights.speaker: Tom Hougaard
insights.so_what: Know your temperament: target-based and trend-adding styles are psychologically incompatible.

insights.claim: David Paul's guideline, as Tom Hougaard relates it, is that a position should be two to three times bigger at the finish than at the start; Hougaard misheard it as 20 to 30 times and traded that way.
insights.speaker: Tom Hougaard
insights.so_what: A concrete pyramiding rule: scale total size as the trend confirms.

insights.claim: Tom Hougaard rejects fixed profit targets because exiting at 40 and watching the market run to 60 hurts him more than taking a smaller exit at 30 after a pullback. He accepts giving back open profit in exchange for the chance of a much larger one.
insights.speaker: Tom Hougaard
insights.so_what: Trailing or discretionary exits suit trend capture; fixed R-multiples cap the right tail.

insights.claim: Tom Hougaard says indicators like stochastics can give traders a subconscious excuse to exit profitable positions early, relieving the pain of holding open profit, and after one such exit the market kept running all day.
insights.speaker: Tom Hougaard
insights.so_what: Audit indicator-driven exits for whether the signal is really an emotional escape hatch.
insights.quote: the stochastics actually stops you from seeing the market for what it is

insights.claim: David Paul's principle, as Tom Hougaard relays it: a single trade's outcome is random, and a statistical edge only shows up over 10 to 100 trades, yet most traders quit after about three straight losses when the amygdala takes over.
insights.speaker: Tom Hougaard
insights.so_what: Judge a strategy on samples of 100 trades, not short streaks; pre-commit to taking the signals.
insights.quote: on the scale of one trade the outcome is completely random. But on the scale of 10 trades that's where statistics kick in

insights.claim: David Capablanca says he no longer uses risk/reward ratios to pick small-cap shorts; his system's exclusions (for example Chinese stocks) screen out bad risk/reward automatically, which he likens to Wall Street desks trading their given criteria.
insights.speaker: David Capablanca
insights.so_what: Rules about what not to trade can replace per-trade R:R math.

insights.claim: As a short seller, David Capablanca uses a long-term thesis about where a pumped small cap 'belongs' to select it, then waits for extension and targets a give-back of most of that extension, re-entering because these stocks 'have nine lives'.
insights.speaker: David Capablanca
insights.so_what: Retail traders' edge over institutions is agility: they can re-short repeated pump cycles in the same ticker.
insights.quote: these stocks they have like nine lives. They just like you know they they drop, they come back.

insights.claim: David Capablanca grades setups A through C. A scalp (B or B-minus) gets half size, split into four 'bullets', while A-plus setups, such as GLD, get full size scaled in across four or five bullets.
insights.speaker: David Capablanca
insights.so_what: Grade setups by quality and size each grade differently, entering in tranches instead of one block.

insights.claim: David Capablanca changes his account size by season: about $50,000-$100,000 in summer (wiring out profits) and $200,000-$500,000 in stronger periods, with a maximum A-setup position anywhere from $50,000 to a quarter million.
insights.speaker: David Capablanca
insights.so_what: Sizing capital at risk to the opportunity season improves returns without changing the strategy itself.

insights.claim: David Capablanca expects a seasonal Thanksgiving and holiday pump-and-dump cycle in small caps, as promoters spread tips during family gatherings, and treats it as an A-plus shorting season.
insights.speaker: David Capablanca
insights.so_what: Watch for holiday-week promotional spikes in small caps as short opportunities.
insights.quote: there's a season to pump and dumps

insights.claim: David Capablanca says he sizes much smaller away from his desk: he shorted NCPL with 2,500 then 5,000 shares from his phone but would have used 10,000 or more on his full setup, and he only does this for stocks he has already researched and 'stalked'.
insights.speaker: David Capablanca
insights.so_what: Mobile or distracted execution should mean smaller size and only on pre-researched names.

insights.claim: Tom Hougaard says scaling up is the same process at larger size and must be built through mental stamina. He cites pit trader 'Rambo' (John Wold Dean), who was 'an awful 20 lot trader', then 40, then 80, until each size became normal.
insights.speaker: Tom Hougaard
insights.so_what: Grow size step by step and accept a period of discomfort at each new level.
insights.quote: winning is easy. The real challenge is losing

insights.claim: Tom Hougaard says that for already-profitable traders, the next level comes neither from error-free execution nor from scaling-in technique, but from never settling, such as refusing to stay at 15 lots once 15 feels comfortable.
insights.speaker: Tom Hougaard
insights.so_what: Above breakeven, the binding constraint is psychological appetite for size, not technique.
insights.quote: it's not about scaling in. It's not about being right or wrong. It's about not being satisfied with where you are right now
